topics: Runbook recap: what we measured this sprint
Continuous batching impact and queue depth patterns
Concurrency target tradeoffs and cap recommendations
KV cache priming and prefix cache hit ratios
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll just kick off. Uh, quick roll call.
[00:07] Samir Patel: Samir here. Hi.
[00:09] Elaine Cho: Elaine.
[00:11] Tom Rivers: Tom.
[00:13] Maya Chen: Maya.
[00:15] Priya Desai: Priya from Redwood.
[00:17] Marco Alvarez: Marco as well.
[00:20] Jordan Lee: Awesome. Ok so goal for today is a short sync — last weekend's throughput run, a couple surprising queue spikes and a retune plan. Priya, can you start with what you saw?
[00:32] Priya Desai: Yeah, sure. So we replayed the 2k RPS burst from Friday with the pilot config you have (the 1x A100 pool), and the continuous batching curve behaved as expected up to about 1.6k RPS. After that we started seeing queue depth grow and p99 jumped from ~320ms to ~700ms in the worst windows. There was also a pattern of small 10-20s tail spikes every 5-8 minutes.
[01:01] Tom Rivers: We saw the same on our side, those spikes lined up with larger payloads — longer instruction templates from the recommender job. Not consistent but correlated with longer context lengths.
[01:15] Priya Desai: Right, so two things: payload distribution variance and concurrency saturation. Our telemetry shows batching latency went up because the runtime kept waiting to hit batch size targets, but the queue started lengthening and the concurrency cap reached the per-model limit. That combination caused the p99 to stretch.
[01:36] Samir Patel: Is that the KV cache thrash? We primed the cache but maybe it's not sticking?
[01:41] Priya Desai: Good question. The KV cache hit ratio during the run was around 67% overall but dropped to low 50s during spikes. We think many requests are using varying prefixes and not hitting the cache. There could also be TTL eviction pressure because of the shorter sequence reuse.
[01:58] Elaine Cho: Just to flag, our platform has bursts of mixed-size requests — about 10% are 3-4x larger. We're trying to avoid dropping them but they seem to be the stomping cause.
[02:09] Jordan Lee: Ok, jump to tradeoffs: we can either lower batch waiting time (emit earlier) to reduce queue depth or lower concurrency targets so we don't overload per-GPU parallelism. Both have cost/latency consequences. Priya, what did modelling show?
[02:24] Priya Desai: If we reduce the batch window from 25ms to 12ms, expected median latency improves by ~30ms on small requests and reduces queue depth, but token throughput efficiency drops — roughly 8-12% more tokens per effective response. If we throttle concurrency cap by 15%, we flatten the batch size distribution and p99 improves but tail throughput dips during sustained bursts.
[02:48] Marco Alvarez: There's also a middle ground: adaptive batch timeout where we reduce wait under high queueing, and allow full batching during steady-state. That's what our continuous batching controller supports — it adapts to observed queue latency.
[03:02] Tom Rivers: That sounds promising if it's stable. We're worried about oscillation though — adaptivity can sometimes overshoot and create jitter.
[03:10] Priya Desai: Totally, which is why we recommend hysteresis thresholds and a short cooldown. The controller we ran had a 15s cooldown and didn't oscillate in our sim, but we saw the cache hit dip which suggests eviction interplay.
[03:23] Maya Chen: Can you expand on the eviction interplay — is it because smaller batches increase number of unique prefixes?
[03:28] Priya Desai: Exactly. When batches are smaller and latency lower, you process different request combinations faster, which increases working set and can reduce effective KV reuse for those slightly longer sessions.
[03:37] Jordan Lee: Samir, what's our success criteria for this sprint? You told us sub-450ms p99 and maintain cost within 10% of baseline, right?
[03:46] Samir Patel: Yep that's still the target. Ideally p95 under 300 and p99 under 450 during 2k burst. Cost we'd like to keep at or under 10% above baseline — because budget is tight.
[03:58] Jordan Lee: Ok, let's go into the concrete retune we propose. Priya?
[04:02] Priya Desai: Proposal A: adaptive batching controller enabled with a tighter batch-window floor of 10ms, 15s cooldown, and a conservative concurrency cap reduction of 10% for the first canary. We also add a KV cache priming script to run for 5 minutes pre-burst to bump hit ratio.
[04:21] Priya Desai: Proposal B: keep current batch settings but enforce a per-route concurrency throttle for heavy payloads and route them to a slightly slower model variant (quantized 4-bit) for large-context requests — darker fallback. That reduces pressure but increases cost complexity and a slight quality delta.
[04:38] Elaine Cho: That second option worries Product — quality delta is risky. Can you quantify the delta?
[04:44] Priya Desai: From our earlier AB, the quantized variant had BLEU-ish/ROUGE-ish style checks show <2% drop on average but with a handful of edge cases that skewed more. For Nextera's recommender prompts, the delta looked tolerable but we'd want to run your eval sets.
[05:00] Samir Patel: We have a small eval set we can share. We'll run it.
[05:04] Jordan Lee: Good. On instrumentation, Tom, we'll need the p99 traces and request size distro. Can you commit to that?
[05:11] Tom Rivers: Yes, I'll pull 48 hours of traces and tag the times of the Friday run.
[05:16] Jordan Lee: Great. Priya, Marco, any quick notes on the priming script?
[05:20] Marco Alvarez: The priming script will replay common prefixes pulled from the Rails of your production logs — it's idempotent and quick. We'll provide the script and a short runbook; it pushes the KV cache into a warm state for about 20-30 minutes. It needs a short headstart.
[05:36] Elaine Cho: Headstart of how long? We can't always schedule 30 min pre-burst.
[05:40] Marco Alvarez: You can do 5 minutes for a partial benefit; ideally 20 minutes for best effect. In the canary we can do a 5-minute priming window to simulate constraints.
[05:48] Maya Chen: Also can we simulate the 10% large payload distribution?
[05:51] Priya Desai: Yes, we'll run a synthetic that overlays a 10% tail of 3-4x length requests; that's part of the 30m burst sim Jordan mentioned in next steps.
[06:00] Samir Patel: About cost, do you have updated estimates for the adaptive controller + 10% concurrency cap?
[06:06] Priya Desai: We project a ~6-9% increase in tokens processed per-response during heavy batching adjustments; but because we cut p99 and reduce repeated retries/fallbacks, net compute minutes should be similar. We'll share a spreadsheet with modeled scenarios.
[06:20] Jordan Lee: We'll attach the scenario sheet. Jordan: (unintelligible) — Samir, you mentioned regional fallback earlier, is Nextera planning multi-region?
[06:29] Samir Patel: We currently run primarily in us-west but have an east region for DR. We don't want cross-region fallbacks for low-latency flows. We'll prefer internal region fallback or dedicated reserved capacity.
[06:39] Priya Desai: For that we can recommend a small warm pool in east region with burst routing only for non-latency-critical workloads. For core low-latency flows we keep within region and do model variant fallbacks.
[06:51] Tom Rivers: One more SRE question: how well does the runtime surface queue depth and batch composition? Our team wants to export metrics into Prometheus.
[06:59] Marco Alvarez: We expose per-route queue_depth, batch_size_histogram, and kv_cache_hit_ratio. We'll provide a Grafana dashboard and Prometheus scrape config.
[07:08] Elaine Cho: Good. That will help debug real-time.
[07:11] Jordan Lee: Ok quick sanity check: can we walk through the canary plan? Priya?
[07:15] Priya Desai: Canary plan: 1) Night window test with 30-minute burst sim (2k target) with 5-minute KV priming. 2) Adaptive batching enabled +10% concurrency cap reduction. 3) Collect p95/p99, batch histograms, KV hit-ratio, and token cost. 4) If p99 < 450ms and cost < 10% of baseline, promote to day run. Otherwise rollback and revert to current config and capture diffs.
[07:39] Samir Patel: Sounds reasonable. What are the rollback triggers?
[07:42] Priya Desai: Rollback if p99 > 750ms in any sustained 5m window or if error rates > 0.5% or if model quality on sample set degrades > 5% per your eval.
[07:53] Maya Chen: We'll need the exact rollback playbook in writing.
[07:56] Jordan Lee: We'll send the playbook after this call.
[07:58] Tom Rivers: For data retention / logs — we'll need the raw request traces for the two canaries. Is that ok from Redwood side?
[08:05] Jordan Lee: Yes, we'll provide temporary signed access and a link to the S3 export. We'll coordinate with Elaine on redaction.
[08:12] Elaine Cho: We'll need SSO integration for the export. Also please confirm audit logs for the run.
[08:17] Marco Alvarez: Export uses the private S3 with pre-signed URLs; audit logs are available and we'll patch the run id to the logs for easy correlation.
[08:26] Samir Patel: Another callout — security/compliance wants confirmation that HSM/KMS keys are customer-managed for Private. We discussed earlier but we need that in writing for procurement.
[08:36] Jordan Lee: We'll put that into the security pack and the SAML/SOC2 sections. I'll attach the specific KMS note.
[08:44] Maya Chen: Great. One last operational detail: what about backpressure on our side — do we need a client-side throttle as well?
[08:51] Priya Desai: It's optional but recommended. A short client-side qps limiter helps smooth peaks and avoids immediate fallback storms; but it's not mandatory if server-side throttles are reliable.
[09:02] Samir Patel: We can add a 5% dampener client-side to help.
[09:06] Jordan Lee: Ok wrapping. Recap — Redwood runs 30m burst sim with KV priming and adaptive batching enabled; Nextera shares traces and eval sets; we schedule canary next week. Action items noted. Anything else?
[09:19] Elaine Cho: None from Platform.
[09:21] Tom Rivers: No.
[09:22] Maya Chen: No.
[09:23] Samir Patel: Thanks.
[09:24] Jordan Lee: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with notes and the runbook.
[09:28] [End of recording]

Notes on transcript fidelity: speaker attribution occasionally generalized (e.g., "Priya" sometimes labeled without role), small transcription errors present ("KV" -> "K V" or "cash"), some punctuation and timestamps approximate.
